title: Adult Upper-Airway Emergency: Stridor, Epiglottitis and Airway Escalation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with stridor or suspected rapidly progressing upper-airway obstruction in the ED: recognition, who to call, what not to do, airway plan, and cause-specific treatment for anaphylaxis and epiglottitis (supraglottitis). Uses the Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) anaphylaxis protocol, Resuscitation Council UK guidance, a hospital antimicrobial policy and a Gulf cohort study.
findings: Rebuilt from the thin 21 Oct 2026 version: four-item presentation lists, diagnostic criteria, six management steps, cause-specific medicine branches, a Saudi source and a guideline comparison added.
Saudi MOH and Resuscitation Council UK differ on adult and paediatric adrenaline doses and fluid volumes; both are shown side by side.
Every dose and threshold traces to a source opened on 22 Oct 2026.
unverifiedSections: No national or international guideline on adult epiglottitis was opened; antibiotics come from a hospital antimicrobial policy (Galway GAPP) and an emergency care summary (Emergency Care BC). Ceftriaxone, the first-listed option, is marked preferred.
Corticosteroids and nebulised adrenaline in epiglottitis: Emergency Care BC finds insufficient evidence; no dose is given here.
Difficult Airway Society plan details (attempt limits, front-of-neck technique) were not opened; the airway plan step follows Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7 only.
Distinguishing features for differentials are clinical descriptions, not taken from an opened guideline section.
Typical adult reference ranges are not from the cited sources; local laboratory ranges apply.
CKD and CLD lines for antibiotics come from the platform batch-01 table and were not re-opened in this task.
SFDA registration was not verified (register not reachable).

pathophysiology.summary: Swelling, infection, a foreign body or a mass narrows the larynx or supraglottis; flow through a narrowed airway produces stridor (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 53). Laryngeal oedema from anaphylaxis or burns can close the airway within minutes (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 53). In adults, infection usually involves the whole supraglottis, not only the epiglottis (Shaikh 2020, Discussion). Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus now outnumber Haemophilus influenzae type b (Matsuura 2017).
keyMechanisms: Narrowed upper airway causes stridor; wheeze points to the lower airway (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 53).
Laryngeal oedema from anaphylaxis or burns can obstruct rapidly (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 53).
Adult supraglottitis involves the epiglottis and surrounding structures (Shaikh 2020, Discussion).
Common adult pathogens: Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (Matsuura 2017).
Complete obstruction in a breathing patient gives see-saw chest and abdominal movement (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 54).

symptoms: Sore throat (89.8% in the Doha cohort) (Shaikh 2020, Results).
Voice change or muffled voice (87.3%) (Shaikh 2020, Results).
physicalSigns: Drooling and sitting upright (Matsuura 2017, p. E1289).
Skin or mucosal changes with hoarseness or stridor suggest anaphylaxis (Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis algorithm).
redFlags: Rapid progression of throat pain, voice change and breathlessness over hours (Matsuura 2017, p. E1289).
Oxygen saturation below 94%, cyanosis or tiring (Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis algorithm).
See-saw breathing or silent chest — complete obstruction (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 54).
Hypotension, confusion or reduced consciousness (Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis algorithm).
Apnoea from complete obstruction occurred in 16.9% of the Doha cohort (Shaikh 2020, Results).
precipitants: Allergen exposure: drug, food or sting (Saudi MOH anaphylaxis protocol, p. 1).
Burns or inhalational injury (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 53).
Foreign body (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 53).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Sudden onset after a trigger with skin changes, wheeze or hypotension (Resuscitation Council UK anaphylaxis algorithm).

differentials.condition: Deep neck infection or Ludwig's angina
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Floor-of-mouth or neck swelling with trismus; it was the commonest complication (28%) of adult supraglottitis in Doha (Shaikh 2020, Results).
Unilateral tonsillar swelling with uvular deviation; needs ear, nose and throat (ENT) drainage (GAPP Throat, quinsy).
Sudden choking onset without fever (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, pp. 54–55).
Expiratory wheeze rather than inspiratory stridor (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, p. 53).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Sudden airway, breathing or circulation problem, usually with skin changes; severe cases may lack skin features (Saudi MOH anaphylaxis protocol, p. 1; Resuscitation Council UK algorithm).
Oedematous epiglottis and supraglottis on flexible nasendoscopy or laryngoscopy (Emergency Care BC; Matsuura 2017).
Thumb sign and loss of the vallecula support the diagnosis; positive in 82.8% of imaged Doha patients (Matsuura 2017; Shaikh 2020, Results).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Stridor, drooling, voice change, see-saw breathing
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Trend drives urgency; a quieter patient may be tiring, not improving.
ruleIn.normalValue: Quiet breathing, normal voice, swallowing secretions

clinicalManagement.title: Call the airway team
actions: Call senior anaesthesia and ENT together (Emergency Care BC).
Keep the patient upright in a position of comfort with humidified oxygen (Emergency Care BC).
Avoid tongue depressors, unnecessary cannulation or other distressing procedures until airway experts are present (Emergency Care BC).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat anaphylaxis if suspected
actions: Give intramuscular adrenaline now; repeat after 5 minutes if no better (Resuscitation Council UK algorithm) — see Medicines.
Remove the trigger; give a crystalloid bolus for hypotension (Resuscitation Council UK algorithm).
Angioedema threatening the airway: intubate immediately by the most experienced person (Saudi MOH protocol, p. 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Oxygenate and prepare
actions: Give high-concentration oxygen; once stable titrate to 94–98% (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, pp. 54 and 58).
Prepare primary and rescue plans including surgical cricothyroidotomy, which gives a cuffed definitive airway (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, pp. 67–68).

clinicalManagement.title: Secure or observe the airway
actions: Airway team decides between observation and intubation; in Doha 39% were intubated, 10.2% could not be intubated and 12.7% had tracheostomy (Shaikh 2020, Results).
Failed intubation and ventilation: surgical cricothyroidotomy (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, pp. 67–68).
Confirm tube position with waveform capnography (Resuscitation Council UK Chapter 7, pp. 64–66).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat the cause
actions: Epiglottitis: ceftriaxone after microbiology advice — see Medicines (GAPP Throat).
Intubated patient: send an epiglottic swab for culture (Emergency Care BC).
Close adult contacts of Haemophilus influenzae type b disease: rifampicin 600 mg orally once daily for 4 days (Emergency Care BC).

clinicalManagement.title: Admit to monitored care
actions: Admit every suspected or confirmed epiglottitis and monitor in the intensive care unit (ICU) (Emergency Care BC).
After anaphylaxis with airway compromise observe at least 6 hours and refer to an allergist-immunologist (Saudi MOH protocol, pp. 3–4).
No discharge from the emergency department (ED) while stridor persists.

regimens.indication: Anaphylaxis with airway swelling, hoarseness or stridor
regimens.dose: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) (Resuscitation Council UK); Saudi MOH gives 0.3–0.5 mg — see Guideline comparison
regimens.frequency: Repeat after 5 minutes if no improvement (Resuscitation Council UK); every 5–15 minutes as needed (Saudi MOH)
regimens.duration: Until airway, breathing and circulation improve; after two intramuscular doses with persisting problems follow the refractory anaphylaxis pathway
adjustments: Intravenous adrenaline only by experienced specialists in an appropriate setting (Resuscitation Council UK algorithm).
Refractory: Saudi MOH infusion starts at 0.1 microgram/kg/minute, titrated to blood pressure, heart rate and oxygenation.
Airway angioedema threatening the airway: intubate immediately by the most experienced person available (Saudi MOH protocol, p. 4).

Penicillin allergy: Sources differ: the BNF advises avoiding it only after anaphylaxis or another immediate reaction to a penicillin (or with any cephalosporin allergy) and otherwise allows use with monitoring; some product information (for example ceftriaxone) lists any penicillin hypersensitivity as a contraindication. Alternative: Immediate or severe penicillin reaction: vancomycin with ciprofloxacin, after microbiology advice (GAPP Throat, acute epiglottitis).

CKD: No dose change if liver function is normal; creatinine clearance below 10 mL/min: maximum 2 g/day — for meningitis doses take pharmacist advice and monitor levels (product information). [batch-01 renal/hepatic table; label not re-opened in this task]

CLD: No dose change if renal function is normal; combined severe renal and hepatic impairment: monitor plasma levels (product information). [batch-01 renal/hepatic table; label not re-opened in this task]
monitoring: Airway: continuous observation in an ICU (Emergency Care BC).
contraindications: Cephalosporin allergy, or anaphylaxis to a penicillin (see Penicillin allergy line).

branches.label: Anaphylaxis with upper-airway compromise
branches.entryCriteria: Sudden airway swelling, hoarseness or stridor after a likely trigger, usually with skin changes

branches.label: Suspected bacterial epiglottitis
branches.entryCriteria: Fever, sore throat, odynophagia, muffled voice or stridor with supraglottic swelling; no anaphylaxis features

branches.label: Epiglottitis with severe penicillin allergy — second agent

medicationPlan.note: Airway control comes first. Branches are cause-specific; do not give both pathways by default. In the epiglottitis branch give ceftriaxone, or vancomycin plus ciprofloxacin in severe allergy — never both. Paediatric, penicillin-allergy, chronic kidney disease (CKD) and chronic liver disease (CLD) lines are on every row; CKD and CLD lines need pharmacist confirmation. SFDA registration not verified.

learningObjectives: Recognise upper-airway obstruction and call the right team at once.
Avoid actions that precipitate complete obstruction.
keyPoints: Stridor means a narrowed upper airway.
Every adult epiglottitis goes to ICU.
pitfalls: Laying the patient flat or examining the throat with a tongue depressor.
Sending an unstable patient to CT.
Reading a quieter airway as improvement.

patientEducation: After anaphylaxis: carry an adrenaline auto-injector when advised and avoid the trigger (Saudi MOH protocol, p. 3).
After epiglottitis: complete the antibiotic course and attend ENT follow-up.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid the identified allergen; read labels for food triggers (Saudi MOH protocol, p. 3).
dischargeCriteria: No stridor; airway reviewed by ENT or anaesthesia.
After anaphylaxis with airway compromise: at least 6 hours of observation (Saudi MOH protocol, p. 4).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Allergy-immunology referral after anaphylaxis (Saudi MOH protocol, p. 3); ENT review after epiglottitis to confirm resolution.
